title: Playing behind soloists rather than soloing
summary: Leeman explains he plays for the soloist and follows phrases, calls Buddy Rich the greatest soloist, and says he knew every breath Wild Bill would take.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well, I may be a drummer, but I can feel what a person is playing -- phrases, I go by phrases. That's why I don't predominate in my drumming, I try to play for the soloist.
That's the reason I'm asking, Cliff.

I try to play behind the soloist, instead of -- that's why I'm not known as a forceful drummistic soloist. I would rather play a four-bar chase, back and forth with a horn and play something a little humorous, something with different tones and sounds, rather than get into a rudimental solo, as some soloists do, you know?

I have to interject here that Buddy Rich is the greatest soloist who lives, and he shall never be capped, as far as I'm concerned. I admire so many others. Anyway, I enjoy feeding you -- you asked me these questions, I'm feeding these people, and I knew every breath
that Wild Bill Davison was going to take, and I still do to this day. That's why he enjoys me working behind him -- because I just won't let him up.
